title: Did Sima Guang Really Smash a Vat? Tracing a Famous Jar Back 900 Years
description:
A 1920s children's storybook says the water vat Sima Guang broke stood "a full five or six feet tall." This episode reads the vessel's record backwards: the History of Song (1345) says "jar," so does Shao Bowen (1132), and the earliest record, the monk Huihong's (about 1118–1121), says jar too; Su Shi's life of Sima Guang leaves the story out. Late-Qing and Republican textbooks swapped jar for vat, and "smashing the vat" may first appear in a 1933 ad. A 2015 TV claim that the Song could not fire so big a vat misses the point: Song records show jars used to pray for rain, and "Please step into the jar" is in Sima Guang's own Zizhi Tongjian. It was a jar: archived. Whether it happened: still open.

Sources are listed below; the 2015 program is paraphrased from a news report. Sentences beginning "we think" are this channel's view.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. Historical figures are drawn as cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant to resemble anyone.

Information as of 2026-10-20

chapters.teacher-book: The 1920s: a storybook describes a huge vat
chapters.yuan-historian: 1345: a Yuan historian writes this passage
chapters.monk-desk: Around 1120: a monk records the scene
chapters.curator-pot: The 17th century: a Jingdezhen brush pot
chapters.tv-collector: 2015: a collector raises doubts on TV

sg101.text: In the 1920s, Shanghai put out a storybook for schoolchildren.

sg102.text: A child falls into a vat of water;

sg103.text: Sima Guang bangs a stone on the vat; clink, clank, water flows out.

sg104.text: The book adds: the vat was huge, a full five or six feet tall.

sg105.text: And it asks: why didn't clever Sima Guang take care of the vat?

sg106.text: Late in the Northern Song, a monk wrote this down, and noted a thing common around the capital.

sg107.text: A man who knew Sima Guang for twenty years wrote his life. Is this story in it?

sg108.text: In the 17th century, a porcelain brush pot showed this scene. How was the vessel drawn?

sg109.text: In 2015, a collector questioned this story on television.

sg110.text: The last clue is hidden in a history compiled in the Song dynasty.

sg111.text: Was it really a vat that Sima Guang smashed?

sg201.text: The official History of Song, finished by the Yuan in 1345, uses a different word.

sg202.text: Kids played in a yard; one climbed a jar, slipped, fell into water;

sg203.text: All fled; Sima Guang broke the jar with a stone, water gushed, the child lived.

sg204.text: One short passage: 'jar' twice, 'vat' not once.

sg206.text: At seven, the History says, he heard the Zuo Zhuan, then retold it at home;

sg207.text: The jar line comes after, with no year in front.

sg208.text: The History of Song came about 320 years after Sima Guang turned seven.

sg210.text: A Southern Song biography skips it: Zuo Zhuan at seven, then his first post.

sg211.text: But earlier still, in 1132, Shao Bowen's Wenjianlu tells it.

sg212.text: His version: a child fell into a big water jar; Sima Guang broke it with a stone; the child got out.

sg213.text: Shao set it beside another childhood tale:

sg214.text: Wen Yanbo flooded a ball out of a hole with water.

sg215.text: He says the wise saw then: both boys were uncommonly kind and wise.

sg216.text: Over 200 years before the History of Song: a jar, again.

sg217.text: But was Shao Bowen the first?

sg301.text: No. About ten years earlier, around 1120, the monk from the start had written it.

sg302.text: He's Huihong; his Lengzhai Yehua is the earliest record found so far.

sg303.text: Sima Guang was then some 30 years dead.

sg304.text: Could this earliest record say vat?

sg305.text: No. He writes: a big jar stood in a yard; a child climbed it and fell into the jar;

sg306.text: Sima Guang hit it with a stone; water spurted out; the child was fine.

sg307.text: Unlike Shao, he didn't write 'broke' but 'knocked a hole'.

sg308.text: No age either, just that Sima Guang was a boy, losing his baby teeth.

sg309.text: That common thing? He names it:

sg310.text: Capital and Luoyang had many paintings of a boy hitting a jar.

sg311.text: Song catalogs called this book unreliable.

sg312.text: So did Huihong make this one up?

sg313.text: A scholar judged it broadly credible, not invented by Huihong;

sg314.text: Shao Bowen lived in Luoyang, his family close to Sima Guang, and he recorded it too.

sg315.text: Did anyone close to Sima Guang write about it?

sg316.text: That man who knew Sima Guang for twenty years was Su Shi.

sg317.text: After Sima Guang died, Su Shi wrote a long account of his life.

sg318.text: Remember the History's line about the Zuo Zhuan at seven? It's nearly verbatim from this.

sg319.text: But the jar that comes right after isn't in it, nor on the tomb inscription.

sg320.text: Why? At the end he explains: anything else unrelated to the realm's order and safety, he left out entirely.

sg321.text: Saving a child: he didn't know, or saw no need to write it.

sg322.text: And Huihong's paintings? Can we still find them?

sg401.text: We found not one. The earliest picture we can see is that brush pot:

sg402.text: 17th-century Jingdezhen blue-and-white, now in America's Cleveland Museum of Art.

sg403.text: The vessel we asked about is painted as a big, wide-mouthed basin, patterned outside.

sg404.text: The Song writers' jar got a wider mouth on porcelain.

sg405.text: And the word 'vat': what was it at first?

sg406.text: The Eastern Han dictionary Shuowen Jiezi, per Xiao Xu and Duan Yucai: a vat is a long-necked clay pot.

sg407.text: Song texts had the word: twice in the History of Song, both for wine;

sg408.text: No Song writer we found telling this story used it.

sg409.text: Today a vat is open-mouthed; narrow mouth, big belly, that's a jar.

sg410.text: So when did the story's jar become a vat?

sg411.text: A scholar who read late-Qing and Republican school textbooks found vat replaced jar from then on.

sg412.text: That storybook's section is titled 'Sima Guang Breaks a Vat to Save a Life.'

sg413.text: The section before it? Wen Yanbo's ball, the one Shao Bowen paired with it;

sg414.text: Even the ball falling into a 'tree hole' matches a Southern Song compendium.

sg415.text: It follows the Song arrangement but swaps jar for vat; it's the earliest vat we've opened.

sg416.text: And when did the phrase 'smashing the vat' appear?

sg417.text: Per a scholar's article, the earliest so far may be a 1933 ad in the Shenbao.

sg418.text: The scholar guesses that from then on, 'Sima Guang Smashes the Vat' became the story's name.

sg419.text: Later, someone used that very vat to question the whole story.

sg501.text: In 2015, the collector from the start argued on the show:

sg502.text: The Song couldn't fire a vat that big, so it never happened.

sg504.text: A scholar replied: using the later 'vat' to question the original 'jar' doesn't even match.

sg505.text: So did the Song have big jars?

sg506.text: In Sima Guang's lifetime, the Xining era, 1068 to 1077, drought hit the capital;

sg507.text: A Song notebook: each lane set out a big jar of water to pray for rain.

sg508.text: The History of Song's rites treatise: drought in summer, Xining 10; the court's rain rite put dozens of lizards in jars.

sg509.text: Neither says how big; what's certain is the capital prayed for rain with jars.

sg510.text: The storybook said five or six feet; but no Song or Yuan text we found gives a jar's height.

sg511.text: Did anyone write of a jar that held an adult?

sg512.text: Yes, famously: the idiom 'Please step into the jar.'

sg513.text: A cruel Tang official suggested a big jar to force confessions; another did just that, then invited him in.

sg515.text: The Zizhi Tongjian. The Song history from the start, compiled by Sima Guang himself, presented in 1084.

sg516.text: It happened in 691, over 300 years before Sima Guang was born.

sg517.text: We think that to Song scholars, a jar that could hold an adult was nothing unusual.

sg518.text: Remember the storybook's question? Why didn't clever Sima Guang take care of the vat?

sg519.text: Because by the records, what he smashed was never a vat. It was a jar.

sg520.text: But did he really save a child as a boy?

sg521.text: In Huihong's book, the entry is titled 'The Art of Saving Lives.'

sg522.text: In the Southern Song, a self-cultivation book took it in, under 'Helping Others.'

sg523.text: Su Shi also records crowds blocking Sima Guang's road: Don't go back to Luoyang! Stay, aid the emperor, save the people!

sg524.text: Was that reputation tied to the childhood story?

sg525.text: A scholar: the tale spread after his death, no coincidence given his fame;

sg526.text: Whether it really happened, that scholar says, can no longer be known.

sg527.text: So this file: one page archived, one page still open.

sg528.text: Your childhood version: vat, jar, or something else?

sg529.text: We only cover what the records hold. Subscribe and open files with us.
